account: A 72-year-old man's below-elbow amputation in 1965 left him with 48 years of phantom limb pain, resistant to mirror therapy, drugs, acupuncture and hypnosis. A team from Chalmers University of Technology and Sahlgrenska University Hospital, both in Gothenburg, treated him. The paper does not name the treatment site. Treatment ran for 18 weeks from March 2013. The exact start date is not reported. Myoelectric pattern recognition classified surface electromyography from his stump, using linear discriminant analysis and a multilayer perceptron in the open-source BioPatRec platform. The decoded movements drove a virtual limb shown in augmented reality and a racing game. After four weeks he reported episodes of lower pain intensity, and after ten weeks near-absent pain developing into completely pain-free periods. His phantom fist relaxed and he could move the phantom freely (Frontiers in Neuroscience, 2014). In December 2016 the same group reported in the Lancet a single-group trial in 14 patients with intractable phantom limb pain, in which pain decreased by 47% for weighted pain distribution. An independent review in 2022 by authors at Loma Linda University and the Department of Veterans Affairs scored the 2014 case report 9 on the MINORS scale and urged caution about the evidence base. In September 2024 the same group reported a double-blind randomized trial in 81 patients at 9 clinics in 7 countries. Pain fell by 64.5% with machine-learning phantom motor execution and by 68.2% with guided motor imagery, and the authors found no evidence that the decoded execution was superior.

ai_role.statement: Pattern-recognition classifiers turned stump muscle signals into predicted phantom movements that a virtual limb carried out. The 2014 authors argue that this overt motor execution drives the relief. In 2024 the same group's randomized trial compared the method with guided motor imagery that decodes nothing and found no difference in pain reduction. The trial does not support a specific benefit from the machine-learning decoding, and the therapy as a whole was followed by large pain reductions in both arms.

fields.account: A 72-year-old man's below-elbow amputation in 1965 left him with 48 years of phantom limb pain, resistant to mirror therapy, drugs, acupuncture and hypnosis. A team from Chalmers University of Technology and Sahlgrenska University Hospital, both in Gothenburg, treated him. The paper does not name the treatment site. Treatment ran for 18 weeks from March 2013. The exact start date is not reported. Myoelectric pattern recognition classified surface electromyography from his stump, using linear discriminant analysis and a multilayer perceptron in the open-source BioPatRec platform. The decoded movements drove a virtual limb shown in augmented reality and a racing game. After four weeks he reported episodes of lower pain intensity, and after ten weeks near-absent pain developing into completely pain-free periods. His phantom fist relaxed and he could move the phantom freely (Frontiers in Neuroscience, 2014). In December 2016 the same group reported in the Lancet a single-group trial in 14 patients with intractable phantom limb pain, in which pain decreased by 47% for weighted pain distribution. An independent review in 2022 by authors at Loma Linda University and the Department of Veterans Affairs scored the 2014 case report 9 on the MINORS scale and urged caution about the evidence base. In September 2024 the same group reported a double-blind randomized trial in 81 patients at 9 clinics in 7 countries. Pain fell by 64.5% with machine-learning phantom motor execution and by 68.2% with guided motor imagery, and the authors found no evidence that the decoded execution was superior.

purpose: Treat phantom limb pain by letting the patient execute phantom movements decoded from stump muscle activity

ratings.reason: A patient with 48 years of treatment-resistant pain reached pain-free periods and regained phantom movement. The case report gives no long-term follow-up, so a lasting effect is not established.

The case report describes one patient. The same group later reported a trial in 14 patients and a randomized trial in 81 patients, and in the randomized trial the authors found no evidence that the decoded execution was superior to guided motor imagery. No realized outcome across a population is documented.
